t: Protecting systems: security measures, backup methods and disaster recovery
l: Hello and welcome to Digital Tech Revision, the podcast for CCEA GCE Digital Technology. I'm Aoife.
And I'm Conor. Today's episode is lesson AP15: Protecting systems: security measures, backup methods and disaster recovery.
So Conor, if someone only remembers one thing from today, what should it be?
Explain how a security policy, authentication, access rights, encryption and firewalls protect data. That is the heart of it.
Okay, take us through it properly.

No single measure keeps data safe, so organisations use layers. Some measures are procedural, such as a security policy that tells staff how to handle data, choose passwords and report incidents. Others are technical: authentication proves that users are who they claim to be, access rights limit what each user can do, encryption makes intercepted or stolen data unreadable, and firewalls filter network traffic. Physical measures, such as locked server rooms, protect the hardware itself.
Makes sense. Keep going.

Even with all of these, data can still be lost through hardware failure, human error, ransomware or a flood, so every organisation also needs to be able to recover. That depends on a sensible backup strategy, using full, differential or incremental backups, and on knowing exactly how to restore from them. For serious incidents that knock out whole systems or buildings, a documented disaster recovery plan sets out what must be restored first, how quickly, by whom and from where. This lesson covers the protective measures, evaluates the three methods of backup, explains how systems are restored, and describes the purpose and contents of a disaster recovery plan.
Right. What else do we need to know?

A security policy is a formal document that sets out the rules, procedures and responsibilities an organisation uses to protect its systems and data. It normally covers acceptable use of equipment and the internet, password requirements, who may access which data, the use of personal devices and removable media, remote working, how to report incidents, backup procedures and the training staff will receive, along with the consequences of breaking the rules. It must be communicated, enforced and reviewed. Access control then turns the policy into practice.
Got it. Keep going.

Users first identify themselves and then authenticate using something they know, something they have or something they are. Multi-factor authentication combines at least two of these factor types, so an attacker who has phished a password still cannot log in without, for example, the user’s phone. Once logged in, access rights determine what each user may do, such as read-only or read and write, and to which files. Following the principle of least privilege limits the damage caused by mistakes, malicious insiders or a compromised account, and audit logs help detect misuse.
And is there anything people often mix up here?

Encryption applies an algorithm and a key to plaintext to produce ciphertext, which cannot be understood without the correct key. In symmetric encryption the same key encrypts and decrypts, which is fast but creates the problem of sharing the key safely. Asymmetric encryption uses a key pair: anyone can encrypt with the public key, but only the holder of the matching private key can decrypt. In practice, asymmetric encryption is used when a secure web connection is set up to agree a symmetric session key, which then encrypts the rest of the traffic. Encryption protects data in transit, such as HTTPS and virtual private networks, and data at rest, such as laptop drives, USB sticks and backups.
Okay. Keep going.

It does not stop data being stolen or deleted; it stops stolen data being read. A firewall examines incoming and outgoing traffic against a set of rules, such as permitted IP addresses, ports and protocols, and blocks anything that does not match. Hardware firewalls guard the boundary of a network, while software firewalls protect individual devices. Anti-malware software and prompt patching complete the technical defences.
Go on.

A full backup copies every file on the system. It is the simplest to restore, because the whole system comes back from a single backup, but it takes the longest to create and uses the most storage, and since only a small fraction of data usually changes each day, most of the copying is repeated work. Many organisations therefore take a full backup weekly and combine it with one of the other methods. A differential backup copies every file altered after the most recent full backup. It is quicker to create than a full backup, and a restore needs only two backups, but each differential is larger than the one before because changes keep accumulating until the next full backup.
Right. Keep going.

An incremental backup copies only the files modified after the most recent backup, whatever its type. It is the fastest to create and needs the least storage, but restoring requires the full backup plus every incremental since, applied in order, so it is the slowest and most complex restore. If any one incremental in the chain is corrupt or missing, later changes cannot be recovered reliably. The best choice depends on how much data changes, the storage available and how quickly the system must be back.
Go on.

A backup is only useful if the organisation can restore from it efficiently, so the restore process must be planned to keep downtime to a minimum. With full backups, the existing files are simply replaced with the most recent full copy, which is straightforward and usually the quickest option. With differential backups, the last full backup is restored first and then the most recent differential is applied; unchanged files come from the full backup and changed files from the differential, which always holds the newest backed-up version of each changed file. With incremental backups, the last full backup is restored and then every incremental made since is applied in date order.
Makes sense. Keep going.

A file may have changed several times, so it may appear in several incrementals, and applying them in order ensures that the latest version ends up in place. In every case the system is then at the state of the last restore point. Any work done after that point is lost unless it was captured in a transaction log, in which case the logged transactions are re-applied to bring the data fully up to date. Restores should be practised regularly so staff know the procedure and can be confident the backups actually work.
Go on.

Disaster recovery is the process by which an organisation recovers its IT systems after a catastrophic event, something much more serious than a single failed disk or deleted file. Disasters may be accidental, such as a fire or widespread data corruption, natural, such as flooding or storm damage, or deliberate, such as a major cyber attack or terrorism. They cannot be prevented, so a disaster recovery plan does not try to avoid them; its purpose is to minimise their effects and allow the organisation to resume operating quickly with as little disruption to customers as possible. The plan should be drawn up when a system is introduced and kept up to date.
Got it. Keep going.

At a minimum it identifies the critical data, the key personnel and their responsibilities, the backup and recovery processes, and a fallback location where work can carry on. The organisation then lists the systems that must be recovered, ranked by importance, and sets a time limit for recovering each one. Techniques to meet those limits include off-site or cloud backups, private online storage, cloud-hosted servers that can be activated on demand and staff on standby. A wider business continuity plan covers keeping the whole organisation running, not just its IT.
Go on.

The CCEA textbook describes the recovery point objectives as the list of parts of the system that must be restored after a disaster, and the recovery time objectives as the time limit for recovering each of them. A retailer might set 12 hours to restore its online shop but five days for payroll, because the shop earns money every hour while staff are paid monthly. In wider industry use, the recovery point objective is usually expressed as the maximum amount of data, measured in time, that the organisation can afford to lose; an RPO of one hour means backups or replication must happen at least hourly. Both views lead to the same practical point: the most critical functions get the highest priority and the most expensive protection.
Okay. Keep going.

A plan that has never been tested may fail when it is needed, so testing is essential. In a walk-through or theoretical test, participants step through the plan to check that everyone knows their role and that contact details and procedures are correct. In a simulation test, working systems are deliberately disabled and actually recovered, so weaknesses such as missing backups or unrealistic time limits are found and fixed before a real disaster.
Time for quickfire key terms. I'll say the term, and you give me the answer the mark scheme gives credit for.
Go for it.
Security policy?
A formal document setting out the rules, procedures and responsibilities an organisation uses to protect its systems and data.
Authentication?
The process of proving that a user is who they claim to be, using something they know, have or are.
Multi-factor authentication (MFA)?
Authentication requiring two or more different types of evidence, such as a password and a code sent to a phone.
Encryption?
Converting plaintext into ciphertext using an algorithm and a key so that it cannot be understood without the correct key.
Firewall?
Hardware or software that monitors network traffic and blocks data that does not meet a set of security rules.
Full backup?
A backup that copies every file on the system, whether or not it has changed, each time it runs.
What about the exam? Where has this come up?

Backup questions often ask you to describe how each method works and give advantages and disadvantages, so learn a precise definition of each: incremental copies changes since the last backup of any type, while differential copies changes since the last full backup. Mixing these up is the most common error. For evaluate questions, compare backup time, storage needed, restore time and the risk of a broken chain, then make a justified recommendation for the scenario. Recovery questions in a context, such as a failure part-way through the week, reward a clear sequence: restore the last full backup, then the relevant differential or each incremental in order, state which point in time the system is now at, then re-apply logged transactions. For disaster recovery plans, the four contents usually credited are the critical data, the key staff, how backups are taken and restored, and a fallback site. When defining RPO and RTO, give the textbook meaning and support it with an example. For security measures, say how the measure works and which threat it counters, and remember that encryption makes stolen data unreadable rather than preventing theft.

Let's finish with a question for the listeners. Which of these should a disaster recovery plan identify? Is it A, The colour scheme of the company website; B, A fallback location where staff can keep working; C, The marketing budget for next year; D, Each customer’s favourite products?
I'll give you a few seconds.
The answer is B: A fallback location where staff can keep working. The core contents are the critical data, the key staff and their roles, how backups are taken and restored, and a fallback site.
